'''Nding''' is an endangered<ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last1=Eberhard |first1=David M. |title=Ethnoloɠue: Languages in Africa and Europe |last2=Simons |first2=Gary F. |last3=Fenning |first3=Charles D. |publisher=SIL International Publications |year=2020 |isbn=978-1-55671-458-0 |edition=23rd |location=Dallas |pages=279}}</ref> [[Niger–Congo]] language in the [[Talodi languages|Talodi]] family of [[Kordofan]], [[Sudan]].<ref name=":2" /> Nding is spoken in the area of the mountain (Jebel) Eliri, on the south of Talodi in South Kordofan, Sudan.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last=Meinhof |first=Carl |date=1965 |orig-date=1910-1919 |title=Eliri |journal=Zeitschrift für Kolonialsprachen |volume=7/9 |pages=36–50}}</ref><ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last=Seligmann |first=Brenda Z. |date=1965 |orig-date=1910-1919 |title=Note on the Language of the Nubas of Southern Kordofan |journal=Zeitschrift für Kolonialsprachen |volume=1/2 |pages=167–188}}</ref> Because of that, the language also goes by the name Eliri.

According to the UNESCO “Atlas of the World’s Languages in Danger” from 2010, the language is critically endangered.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |title=Atlas of the world's languages in danger |date=2010 |publisher=Unesco |others=Christopher Moseley, Alexandre Nicolas, Unesco, Unesco. Intangible Cultural Heritage Section |isbn=978-92-3-104095-5 |edition=3rd ed. entirely revised, enlarged and updated |location=Paris |oclc=610522460}}</ref>

== Phonology ==

=== Vowels ===
In the Nding language, exist the following vowels: ''a, e, i, o, u''. Among those ''a, e, o,'' can be further classified as long or short, pronunciation-wise.<ref name=":2" />

=== Consonants ===
In the Nding language, appear following consonants: ''k, g, ṅ, tj, dj, ń, t, d, n, r, l, y, p, b, m, w''.<ref name=":2" /> Interestingly, the sound “''h''” is absent in Nding.<ref name=":2" /> Consonants can be nasalized by connecting one consonant with ''n'' or ''m;'' and in some cases, also with their various parallel forms, e.g. ''ṅg'' (alternatively ''ńg''/''ṅń)'', ''ndj'' (alternatively ''ṅdj''/''ńdj''), ''nd, mb''.<ref name=":2" /> Rarely does one come across such combinations as ''rn, rb, dr''.<ref name=":2" />

The consonant “''l''” [el] can, and often is, also written as “''il''”.<ref name=":2" />

=== Consonant and vowel changes ===
Words can change from voiceless to voiced if the preceding word ends with “''n''”. For example, ''tetjo'' [eng. house] in the sentence “the man departs from the house” becomes ''detjo'': ''babura ako a'''n''' '''d'''etjo''.<ref name=":2" /> Such consonant and vowel changes also seem to happen in an irregular manner, as there is no obvious connection found yet, e.g. ''tj'' becomes ''dj'', ''ti'' becomes ''di'', ''ta'' becomes ''da''.<ref name=":2" />

=== Tonality ===
There is no evidence of tones in Nding.<ref name=":2" />

== Grammar ==

=== Sentence structure ===
The most widespread sentence structure seems to be Subject→Verb→Object, however, the use of Verb→Object→Subject has been documented as well.<ref name=":2" /> Personal pronouns come before the verb.<ref name=":2" /> Prepositions such as “what” (Nding: ''yara''), “where” (Nding: ''ča'') and “who” (Nding: ''abura'') come at the beginning of the sentence.<ref name=":3" /> Important is the fact that the noun doesn't change, no matter its usage, e.g. the noun being a subject/an object/when it comes together with a preposition, has no influence on its form.<ref name=":3" />

=== Nouns ===
Nouns seem to be mostly voiceless, but when they become adjectives, they usually (but not always) become voiced, e.g. ''p'' becomes ''b'', ''tj'' becomes ''dj''.<ref name=":2" />

==== Genus ====
Gender of a noun is signaled in Nding through prefixes.<ref name=":2" /> For more information, see the paragraph below.

==== Plural forms ====
The plural form is created through a change of the initial sound of the noun and it depends on the gender-bound prefix, that the noun possesses.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":3" /> That can mean a change of the prefix or a change of the final position of the word.<ref name=":2" /> The before-mentioned categories stand at the core of Meinhof's plural form classification. First, I'll talk about the prefix-changing building of the plural form. There are the following subcategories of these nouns, according to Meinhof:<ref name=":2" />

# sing. ''b''- pl. ''y''- (e.g. sing. ''baà'' pl. ''ya'' [eng. a man]) and sing. ''p''- pl. – (e.g. sing. ''pali'' pl. ''ali'' [eng. a pot])
# sing. ''dj''- ''tj''- ''t''- pl. ''m''- (e.g. sing. ''tino'' pl. ''mino'' [eng. a rock, stone])
# sing. ''t''- pl. ''r''- or ''n''-
# sing. ''g''- or – pl. ''ṅ''- (attention! sing. ''ṅu-'' pl. ''ṅa''-)
# sing. ''tje''- and – pl. ''kā''-
# sing. ''k''- pl. –

Now, the other type of plural form, created by a change of the final position, is categorized in the following way:<ref name=":2" />

# sing. -''ak'' or -''k'' pl. ''a''- or –

Oftentimes vowel changes appear in plural forms too, e.g. ''nu'''dru'''ba'' pl. ''nu'''duru'''ba'' [eng. rabbit].<ref name=":2" />

Plural forms can also change their stems and be irregular, e.g. sing. ''bwai'' pl. ''tje'' [eng. cow/cows].<ref name=":2" />

=== Adjectives ===
The information and data gathered on the topic of adjectives are very limited, and according to Seligmann, in Nding they would be usually replaced with a verbal construction, e.g. instead of saying “no mountain is greater than Eliri” it would be literally translated as “no mountain surpasses Eliri”= ''ko ma keñe Dayo''<ref name=":3" />''.''

The initial sound of an adjective adapts to the initial sound of the noun, to which it refers to, and they change in their plural forms accordingly.<ref name=":2" /> Meinhof divided the adjectival noun-dependent prefixes into 3 categories:<ref name=":2" />

# sing. ''b''- and ''p''- pl. ''y''- or – (e.g. -''abuya'' [eng. full]→ sing. '''''p'''ali '''b'''abuya'' pl. ''ali '''y'''abuya'' [eng. a full pot/full pots])
# sing. -''ōte'' [eng. good] (e.g. sing. '''''tj'''alaṅga '''dj'''ōte'' pl. '''''m'''alanga '''m'''ōte'' [eng. a good leg/good legs]). Here one can also notice how the ''tj''- and ''dj''- prefixes have the same, beforementioned plural prefix form ''m''-
# -''akonda'' [eng. broken] (e.g. sing. '''''g'''uri '''k'''akonda'' pl. '''''n'''uri '''n'''akonda/e''). Attention to exceptions; As one can see, the adjective and the noun in the singular form don’t fit exactly (''g'' and ''k'') but in the plural, they both start with the same letter (''n'')

=== Case ===
The genitive seems very rare and almost non-existent in the Nding language, however, when it is used, it is put at the end of the phrase unit, just like in Bantu, e.g. ''ba bura bá Dayo'' [eng. an Eliri man/a man from Eliri].<ref name=":2" />

The numerals 1,2 and 3 with connection to the -''mena'' (see numbers 6, 7, 8) gain an initial sound -''y''. It is being theorized, that -''mena'' means something like “add”.<ref name=":2" /> Additionally, the number 10 (''yemeńunok'') and the repeated ''"yemenyalok"'' in the number 20, are thought to be the same word (''ń→ny'' and ''u→a'').<ref name=":2" />

=== Pronouns ===

==== Personal pronouns ====
Normal personal pronouns: ''aṅi'' (I), ''aṅo'' (you), ''aṅo'' (he), ''arnaṅo'' (we), ''ata'' (they).<ref name=":2" />

Personal pronouns before the verb: ''ńi/ṅi/ni'' (I), ''aṅo'' (you), ''aṅo'' (he), ''ṅori/ari'' (we), ''ṅorno/ano'' (you pl.), ''ṅota''/''ӑtӑ'' (she).<ref name=":2" />

Personal pronouns can also conjoin with the verbs and act as suffixes; thus, indicating the subject of the action: -''ia/i'' (I), -''wa/o'' (you), -''wa/oba'' (he), -''uria/-ori'' (we), -''ota/-ata'' (you pl.), -''una/-ata'' (she).<ref name=":2" /> When that happens, the stem of the word can change (esp. the vowels ''a, o, u'' have a tendency to swap).<ref name=":2" /> Nevertheless, there are many ambiguities and contradictions in the data about personal pronouns, so there are still many problems with finding a clear pattern.<ref name=":2" />

==== Possessive pronouns ====
Personal pronouns: ''i/iṅ/ńe'' (my/mine), -''a'' (your/yours), -''oba'' (his), -''ori'' (our), -''ono/-ai'' (your/yours), -''ano/-ota'' (her).<ref name=":2" />

==== Interrogative pronouns ====
''Interrogative pronouns: abura'' (who), ''bi'' or ''yara'' (what), ''tja'' (where).<ref name=":2" />

=== Verbs ===

==== Verbal suffixes ====
See the paragraph above on personal pronouns.

==== Negation ====
Negation is accomplished by the use of a post-position ''ma/nā/nӑ''.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":3" />

==== Imperative form ====
The information about the imperative form is also somewhat unclear, but as one sees in the following example, it has been observed, that there is surely a difference between an imperative in a singular form and in the plural (a suffix -''ano'' is gained in the plural): ''ŭṅo!'' (you go!) ''uṅano!'' (pl. you go!).<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":3" />

==== Past tense ====
Exemplary conjugation of a phrase "to break a stick": ''koñi guri'' (I broke a stick), ''koño guri'' (you broke…), ''koñoba guri'' (he broke…), ''koñori guri'' (we broke..), ''koñata guri'' (you [pl.] broke…), ''koñata guri'' (they broke..).<ref name=":3" />

=== Adverbs ===
Adverbs: ''nĕnna'' (here), ''tegu'' (yesterday).<ref name=":2" />

=== (Pre- and post-)positions ===
Postpositions: ''ma/nā/nӑ'' (used for negation).<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":3" />

Prepositions: ''ra'' („in“ in a sense, when someone is asking for a location of something), ''ba'' („to“), ''an'' („from“), ''nā'' („at/on“), ''tuko'' („outside“), ''tuka'' („at/on“ in a sense, when someone asks about location), ''djeta'' (“far from”), ''noṅgotjon'' (“close to”), ''tenyagan'' (“under”), ''ti/tiaritjo'' (“in the middle of”).<ref name=":2" />
